boards.name: 02 / Getting pad information onto the screen / Desktop / Light

text.name: Article title
text.text: Getting pad information onto the screen

text.name: Description
text.text: A working text renderer still needs a route from the real screen. R2 taught us to test both.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We replaced the large BPM display with a compact information panel. The first attempt passed its local tests and changed nothing the owner could see. Following the active screen's redraw route led to the working R2 build.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: R2 tests the current draw route and uses a distinct menu marker. The owner confirms the marker and panel.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic sequence with invented sample data. The owner confirmed that R2 displayed pad information; no device photograph or installed-image readback was captured. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Timeline title
text.text: From a renderer to a visible panel

text.name: Heading
text.text: Choose information that fits the screen

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: After the first menu-title change, we wanted the screen to say something useful about the selected sample. A compact panel could show its name, source tempo, duration and playback settings without requiring a separate menu. Keeping that panel tied to the current selection was part of the feature: changing pads or banks should change the information.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The labels needed precise meanings. SRC is the stored source BPM, which can differ from the tempo heard during playback. LEN is the trimmed source duration before playback-speed changes. ST and MO describe stereo or mono; G, L and R show gate, loop and reverse. R2 limits the name to 17 printable ASCII characters and gives an empty pad an explicit EMPTY PAD state. These choices keep the drawing bounded even when the sample record is unusual.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Find why the passing build changed nothing

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The first candidate passed 528 native display cases and 804 comparisons involving the event handler. The owner then reported that the update had completed but the pads still showed the same large number. The tests and the report appeared to disagree because they were checking different paths.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R1's tests called an older page renderer and its event handler directly. Those calls established what our code did when invoked. The current sample screen used a different widget and redraw dispatcher, so the visible screen never reached the custom panel through that route. We preserved R1 and wrote a regression that began at the current widget's draw entry. It reached the stock BPM renderer without entering R1's custom drawing code. That reproduced the routing mistake locally, although it could not establish the exact bytes installed on the owner's unit.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A renderer test should answer two questions: does the function draw correctly, and does the real screen call that function?

text.name: Heading
text.text: Add the panel to the current redraw

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R2 kept the current widget's stock renderer and event handlers intact. Its wrapper let the stock rendering run, then drew the compact information panel through the current widget's canvas. The dispatcher could continue drawing its header and status areas. External-control behavior remained outside the new panel's normal path.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The correction also removed the earlier event hook. This reduced the number of altered paths we had to explain and kept selection behavior with the existing handler. The revised CPU checks exercised 480 selection notifications followed by current-widget redraws, covering all 160 pads across three layouts. Another 524 detail cases covered formatting and boundary behavior. Drawing APIs and several stock operations were intercepted, so these remained CPU checks with synthetic records, not an emulated OLED, scheduler or audio engine.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Start a routing test at the entry used by the current screen.

2. Keep the original drawing and event behavior in the expected call sequence.

3. Exercise selection changes as well as one direct draw.

4. Check empty and invalid records before considering a device result.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Give the result a visible identity

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R1 reused CUSTOM MENU!, the marker from the earlier title-only experiment. That made a report of the title ambiguous. R2 introduced PAD INFO R2! so the owner could identify the candidate independently of whether the new sample panel appeared.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner initially reported CUSTOM MENU! again, then clarified that the wrong build had been running and confirmed both PAD INFO R2! and the pad information. This was a separate mistake from R1's missed route. Combining the two into one story would hide a real code defect behind an installation mix-up. The hardware report records the correction while leaving the original packages and their build-time reports unchanged.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Keep the success narrower than the feature list

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner's confirmation supports successful execution and a visible pad-information panel on their SP. No independent screenshot or installed-image hash was captured. Individual field accuracy, all banks and layouts, playback behavior and long-session stability still needed separate hardware checks.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: You can reproduce the formatting and routing distinction below without owning an SP or obtaining a firmware image. The example uses invented records and an ordinary Python function table. Its route names explain the test structure; they are not interfaces to the instrument. The retained project reports identify the historical builds and CPU checks, but the underlying research records are not public downloads from this site.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Check the text and the route separately

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Run this standalone Python 3 example. It reads invented in-memory sample data and prints a bounded panel, then checks whether a simulated current screen reaches the custom renderer. It does not access an SP or any files.

text.name: Command
text.text:
Dry kick
SRC 120.00 ST
LEN 1.25s
G:1 L:0 R:0
R1 current route: missed
R2 current route: reached

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: The duration follows from 60,000 source frames at 48,000 frames per second. Passing the panel assertions says nothing about which renderer a screen calls. The final two lines make that second check explicit. The flag line is fixed example data, not a decoder for Roland's sample records.

text.name: Evidence text
text.text:
CPU checks + owner-reported display. The reports below are retained project records; their underlying files are not published here. Read the curated evidence record.

The timeline is schematic and its sample values are invented.

The owner confirmed the panel on one unit; no photograph or installed-image hash was captured.

CPU checks do not establish physical field accuracy, audio behavior or long-session stability.

The exercise reproduces a test structure, not firmware modification or installation.

boards.name: 03 / Making AntiWorkProTwerk move / Desktop / Light

text.name: Evidence label
text.text:
Original renderer trace + owner report
September 22, 2026

text.name: Description
text.text: The first working animation joined an integer renderer, owned widget state and the screen's existing redraw callback.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R3 put the rotating AntiWorkProTwerk logo on pad 1. Its preserved renderer frames are the same source used by the OpenSP homepage. The owner reported that it worked; the browser's playback timing is still an assumption.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: Other pads retain R2's sample-information display. The owner confirms visible continuous animation.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Replay of pixel calls from the compiled original ARM renderer, not a recording of the SP. The trace omits the stock font, caption, header and surrounding UI. Its 50 ms frame interval is a preview assumption, not measured device timing.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Once R2 could draw useful sample information, we had a working place for a more visible experiment. R3 gave the first pad in each bank a rotating two-line logo: AntiWork above ProTwerk. Other pads kept the information panel. Selecting pad 1 was enough to keep the animation moving while that screen stayed active; it did not depend on repeatedly pressing the pad.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The original design used a 36 by 14 cell grid and three depth layers. Integer projection placed the text at 64 angles, with small pixel patterns standing in for ASCII-style marks. Perspective and a slight tilt gave the letters depth. The renderer avoided a floating-point library, and the animation reused the widget's existing periodic callback instead of creating another animation task.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Put the angle inside the widget

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A single frame can be drawn from its inputs. An animation also needs to remember where it was. R3 extended the widget's allocation from 228 to 232 bytes and initialized the added word when the widget was constructed. That word held the phase, so its lifetime followed the screen object that used it.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The periodic wrapper ran the original callback first. When pad 1 was selected outside external-control mode, it advanced the phase and requested a redraw through the existing dirty-notification helper. Selecting another pad stopped that advance. Returning to pad 1 resumed the retained phase; reconstructing the widget reset it. The tests checked allocation and initialization together, because adding a field without guaranteeing its storage would make an otherwise correct renderer unsafe.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Treat allocation, initialization and the callback that updates state as one contract. Testing the drawing function alone leaves the animation's lifetime unchecked.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Check a cycle and the paths around it

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The local tests produced 64 distinct renderer frames and exercised 128 callback invocations, enough to cross the phase boundary twice. They also compared 450 other-pad cases with R2 so the new logo would not silently replace the information panel everywhere. Bank changes, layout variants and external-mode behavior were part of the bounded checks.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R3 needed more room than R2's small reservation. Its implementation used a separate code-and-constant section, which made the builder's view of placement important. An initial address was four bytes before the linker's emitted aligned section. Inspection caught the mismatch before delivery, and the builder gained a check against the actual section address. A separate test expectation missed an external-mode query made by the callback; that expected trace was corrected. Neither finding was a hardware failure.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Render every phase and check that the captured frames are distinct.

2. Advance through wraparound and verify that state stays in range.

3. Compare unaffected pad paths with the preserved R2 behavior.

4. Verify the emitted build's layout instead of assuming the linker kept a requested placement.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Separate the owner result from the preview

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Asked whether the R3 marker and continuously spinning logo worked, the owner replied, "yes r3 completely worked". That supports boot and visible animation on their SP, including this widget-state and periodic-redraw path. There was no independent installed-image readback or screen photograph, and the report did not measure frame rate, timing margin or long-session behavior.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The replay on this page comes from pixel calls captured while executing the compiled original ARM renderer. It preserves the 64 renderer frames, but omits the stock font, caption, header and surrounding UI. Its 50 ms interval gives a 3.2-second browser cycle. That interval was chosen for the preview and has not been established as the physical SP's frame timing. A recognizable replay is useful evidence of the drawing code without being a device recording.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Keep the sequence separate from the instrument

boards.name: 04 / Building a diagnostic capture we could trust / Desktop / Light

text.name: Article title
text.text: Building a diagnostic capture we could trust

text.name: Description
text.text: A failed task, a corrected stack and the checks behind our first useful boot-region capture.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Before we could build an original application, we needed to understand the program that starts it. R5 produced the first validated resident capture after R4 failed before it read any boot memory.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: The session identifies R5. The shared file format cannot identify the producing build by itself.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic stages of the R4/R5 investigation. These screen labels explain the evidence; they are not a device recording or a copy of the diagnostic UI. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Timeline title
text.text: From a failed task to checked bytes

text.name: Heading
text.text: Find the program before the application

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The application download told us a great deal about the sampler, but it did not contain the resident program responsible for starting and updating that application. We needed evidence from the running instrument to investigate that boundary. The diagnostic was limited to a fixed read of the resident window and a file that a PC could check afterward.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A useful capture needed more than a plausible filename. The diagnostic first exercised storage with a known pattern, checked a known application slice, copied the resident window and read the completed file back. Those checks gave us ways to reject a partial file or an obvious mismatch before treating its contents as evidence. This chapter explains those checks without distributing the captured firmware.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner reached the diagnostic start path and reported FAILED, E7 -33. That error came from task creation: the kernel's automatic stack allocator had returned no usable block for the requested 8 KiB stack. The worker never started, so the attempt had not reached storage access or boot-memory reads. There was no capture to inspect.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Our original tests had intercepted task creation. They could exercise the worker while overlooking whether the real task allocator could launch it. The correction was to test the actual creation instructions with an empty automatic allocator and preserve the failed R4 build. The failure did not tell us how much total RAM was free or establish an SD-card problem.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Identify the first failed stage before investigating later ones. A task-creation error cannot establish a file-write failure.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R5 obtained memory from the application's variable memory pool and supplied an aligned 8 KiB span to task creation. It did not choose an apparently unused address. Tests covered all eight starting alignments, allocation failures and cleanup failures, then repeated task creation without using the allocator that had rejected R4.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The allocation stayed owned until reboot after a successful start. A worker cannot free the stack it is still executing on, and the displayed DONE state comes before the task has finished exiting. Limiting the diagnostic to one attempt per boot bounded that retained allocation. Failure cleanup also had to respect whether a dormant task still owned the stack. The capture worker itself kept the R4 format and behavior.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Check the supplied file in layers

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: After the R5 instructions, the owner supplied a 524,880-byte file. Its header, footer, expected length, deterministic storage pattern and complete-body CRC passed the PC verifier. The 256-byte known application slice also matched stock v5.52 byte for byte. The file differed from the synthetic test fixture and contained a full 524,288-byte resident window.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Readable startup structures, updater strings and code made the result useful for further analysis. Strings alone did not establish which paths actually ran. One header field declared a 4 MiB image length; that was neither the amount captured nor a measurement of the flash chip's physical capacity. We kept the original file, its hashes and the validation report together so later interpretations could return to the same bytes.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Reject a wrong total length or missing structural marker.

2. Verify the known pattern and checksum coverage.

3. Compare the known application bytes against the expected version.

4. Preserve the original file and record how it was obtained before interpreting unknown content.

text.name: Heading
text.text: A valid file still needs a history

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R4 and R5 shared the same capture format, which had no unique build ID, device serial or timestamp. The file's integrity checks therefore could not identify the installed revision. R5 attribution came from the installation conversation and the location where the owner supplied the file. Keeping that distinction explicit prevented a checksum pass from becoming an unsupported claim about origin.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Together, the owner report and valid file supported one successful R5 task, storage and boot-read run. They did not test every cancellation path, repeated boots, audio behavior or failed-image recovery. The resident content then gave us a basis for studying application startup. Installing a replacement resident program remained outside what this capture had established.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Run this standalone Python 3 example. It creates an invented note format entirely in memory, then checks a truncation, a changed byte and a newly checksummed replacement. It reads no firmware and writes no files.

text.name: Command
text.text:
original: valid
truncated: length mismatch
changed: CRC mismatch
replacement: valid
producing build: unknown

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: The replacement passes because its checksum agrees with its own bytes. Neither valid result identifies who produced the note or which program made it. The real diagnostic format and checks were more extensive; this small fixture reproduces only that distinction.

text.name: Evidence text
text.text:
Owner report + verified capture. The reports below are retained project records; their underlying files are not published here. Read the curated evidence record.

One successful capture does not establish repeated-run reliability, cancellation behavior or audio stability.

The shared R4/R5 format cannot independently identify the producing revision.

A readable resident capture does not establish independent recovery or permission to replace resident, APP0 or security settings.

The exercise validates an invented in-memory format; it does not reproduce the physical capture or authorize a device operation.

boards.name: 05 / Our first original application / Desktop / Light

text.name: Description
text.text: What R6 and R7 established about starting our own code, drawing a screen and responding to the power switch.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R6 put a source-built application on the SP's display. R7 brought quick startup and working shutdown, while the missing pad response led us toward a separate input driver.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: The owner confirms working shutdown. Its physical completion is an owner report, not a photograph of the exchange.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic evidence states for R6 and R7. The sequence compresses separate observations; its timing and screen composition are illustrative. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Timeline title
text.text: What the first boots actually showed

text.name: Heading
text.text: Give the first boot a small job

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Our earlier changes ran inside Roland's application. The next candidate replaced APP1 with a small original program built from source, while retaining the stock resident program and APP0. Its job was to put an identifiable title on the display, advance a heartbeat and expose a few observations about startup and incoming traffic. It had no sample playback or project browser.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The preserved R6 application was 4,340 bytes. CPU tests could check pieces of its startup and modeled display output, but the physical screen still needed a device result. The visible ORIGINAL R6 marker helped connect the owner's report to the intended package. We did not have an independent on-device hash or readback for this early test.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Wait before calling it a button response

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner initially saw the screen after pressing pad 1 and wondered whether a button had woken it. They then corrected the observation: the display appeared automatically after roughly 20 seconds. The pad and button lights were already on. We preserved both reports and withdrew the button-wake explanation.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Once the screen appeared, ALIVE increased and the bottom bar progressed. That supported physical boot and continued execution of our application and display driver. Pads did not change the screen. Moving the power switch to OFF also left the unit awake, requiring power removal. R6 did not handle the controller's shutdown request. The exact cause of its startup delay was still unproven.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: For a suspected input response, repeat the observation without touching the control. Record what changes automatically before attributing a change to your action.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Make each counter answer one question

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A rising receive counter established that traffic arrived. It did not establish pad input, correct packet alignment or a working control map. R6 also showed a receive error. Those observations called for better visibility into the packets and their timing instead of interpreting every change as a button event.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R7 added interrupt-driven receive handling, explicit timer and ready-input setup, packet history and the traced shutdown reply. The display distinguished frames, received packets, interrupt entries and received bytes. This gave a later photograph enough context to compare a physical action with a specific change, even when the higher-level event counter remained zero. The program still lacked the local pad and knob drivers.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Use a unique visible build title so feedback has a clear candidate.

2. Keep heartbeat, raw traffic and interpreted events in separate fields.

3. Preserve the state before and after one physical action.

4. Check normal shutdown independently of successful screen drawing.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Compare the photographs with the report

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner reported quick automatic startup, an advancing progress bar and working power-off in R7. Three photographs showed its title and captured the initial state, SHIFT press and SHIFT release. Each SHIFT edge added one four-byte packet, four received bytes and four interrupt-handler entries. The timer-progress flag and configured ready-input flag both read one.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: An early description said TX was changing. The photographs corrected our interpretation: the adjacent received-byte counter changed while the transmit-failure counter stayed zero. One framing error remained unchanged across the images. Recognizable SHIFT packets did not establish that error recovery always worked, and a moving timer did not measure its frequency. The shutdown result came from the owner's report; the photographs did not capture the power exchange.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Follow the missing controls to their own path

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Only SHIFT affected the input display. The corresponding stock trace connected those packets to SHIFT's press and release handlers, while separate GPIO and analog routines supplied local controls. R7 had not implemented those routines. The next input work therefore needed a local scan, followed by physical mapping, instead of assuming all controls would arrive over the controller link.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R6 and R7 established increasingly usable original-application bring-up on the owner's instrument. They still depended on Roland's resident program and APP0, had no sampler or audio features, and had no demonstrated failed-image recovery at this milestone. Later recovery results belong to their own tests. We kept these early packages and reports unchanged so later success would not erase what was missing here.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Run this standalone Python 3 model with invented event times. It separates waiting for readiness, advancing the application and handling a stop request. It performs no device access and does not model the SP's electrical timing or controller protocol.

text.name: Command
text.text:
ready + stop: stopped after 4 frames
no readiness: startup timeout
no stop request: running, 7 frames

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: A readiness event lets the model advance, and a missing event ends in a bounded timeout. Stopping needs its own handled event. These tests cover the invented state machine only; they cannot establish physical boot, a measured startup delay or working power removal.

text.name: Evidence text
text.text:
Owner reports + R7 photographs. The reports below are retained project records; their underlying files are not published here. Read the curated evidence record.

R6 and R7 package identity rests on reported or photographed titles, without an independent device hash/readback.

The roughly 20-second R6 delay is an owner observation; its exact cause was not established.

R7 photographs support SHIFT packet observations, while successful shutdown is separately owner-reported.

These candidates retained stock resident/APP0 and had no sampler, audio or demonstrated failed-image recovery at this milestone.

The in-memory exercise reproduces a small state-machine check, not the original firmware or a hardware installation.

text.name: Evidence label
text.text:
Owner-labeled captures and offline replay
September 22, 2026

text.name: Description
text.text: From moving bars to 55 accepted mappings, with one control at a time and the raw recordings kept for review.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Our original application could see buttons and changing analog values. We still needed to establish which reading belonged to which control. The mapping session produced 55 accepted names, caught an incomplete checklist and exposed eight readings for a single DEL button.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: The completed session retained 55 mappings and all 63 takes, including retries.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic mapping sequence. Screen text explains the method; it is not a recording of the R12 interface or its timing. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Timeline title
text.text: From a raw channel to a control

text.name: Heading
text.text: Start with a response we can observe

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R7 responded to SHIFT over its controller link, but the pads and other panel controls needed separate local acquisition. R8 added button-matrix scanning and analog readings. The owner reported that the buttons and knobs did something, and that pressure or turning changed the bars. That gave us a working raw-input baseline on the SP.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The bars had no trustworthy physical names yet. A changing channel could show that acquisition worked without telling us whether it belonged to PAD 1, VOLUME or another control. Pressure-responsive readings also did not establish strike velocity. We preserved R8 and moved the naming work into a recorder where each proposed label could be checked against its raw take.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Record one physical action at a time

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R12 exposed timestamped raw observations over USB. Its capture health included dropped events and ADC errors, so a plausible-looking trace could still be rejected if collection had failed. The guide began each take with a two-second quiet baseline. The owner then moved the named control while leaving the others alone and reviewed the candidate before accepting it.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Keeping the unprocessed take let us recompute the candidate later. The physical name came from the owner's selected action; the recording alone could not identify the hand on the panel. For a knob, the activity covered its travel and return. Buttons were pressed and released twice. Repeating a no-signal take was useful, but a second failure stayed unresolved instead of acquiring a guessed label.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A mapping needs a labeled action, a usable baseline and a healthy capture. A changing value by itself supplies only one of those.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Fix the checklist without changing the firmware

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The first session accepted 22 controls: all 16 pads, CTRL 1 through 3, VALUE rotation and press, and SHIFT. Then the guide stopped. It had omitted VOLUME and the remaining buttons, so calling that session a complete panel map would have hidden a problem in our own instructions.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R12B revised only the PC guide. It resumed the saved profile, kept the accepted labels and prompted for the missing controls. The owner subsequently reported that the checklist was finished. The combined archive contains 55 unique accepted mappings and all 63 takes, including retries. Every take reported zero capture drops and ADC errors; the UART error count remained at one.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Explain the exceptions before using the map

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: VOLUME mapped to analog slot 16. SUB PAD mapped to analog slot 20 and needed pad behavior, correcting the checklist's button classification. An intermediate SUB PAD take had captured EXT SOURCE instead; later corroborating takes superseded it. Keeping that mistaken take made the correction traceable.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: DEL produced the same row response in all eight matrix columns. Treating each candidate as an independent button would duplicate actions. The observed pattern agreed with the stock mapping's column-zero rule, so the named layer uses slot 4 and ignores its seven aliases. Offline replay then produced the expected two DEL press/release pairs. This established a handling rule for the observed pattern without claiming that we had inspected the board wiring.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Freeze what is known and leave gaps visible

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: All accepted candidates could be recomputed from the saved samples, and each accepted mapping emitted the expected event type in offline replay. That check made the map useful for the next native decoder. It remained a single-device, owner-labeled result; replaying a recording was not a second physical test.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: GAIN's saved take had no candidate. MIC/GUITAR was skipped without a take. Neither result proved those controls were analog-only or inaccessible. VALUE's valid state transitions did not establish detents, direction or missed cycles at speed. Pad pressure readings still needed calibration, and a threshold crossing could occur while a finger remained on the pad. Those limits traveled with the map into the next build.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Find a candidate and suppress aliases

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Run this standalone Python 3 example with invented in-memory readings. Its 64-count candidate threshold is illustrative. It performs no device access and writes no files.

text.name: Command
Checkpoint note
text.text: The quiet channel stays out of the candidate list. Counting every alias would produce 16 press events; consuming the selected canonical slot produces two. Real multi-candidate takes require investigation before applying an alias rule. These invented traces do not reproduce the SP's scan timing.

The labels rely on the owner's actions on one SP; the guide does not establish every unit's wiring.

text.name: Article title
text.text: From a RAM upload to a booted update

text.name: Description
text.text: How a working USB connection became a verified persistent update, with a failed compatibility check in between.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R9 received a program into memory. R11 eventually stored a different program and booted it. We needed separate evidence for every step between those two results.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: After a real restart, the owner saw USB BOOT R11 and USB reported the proof's distinct marker with fresh idle state.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic status sequence, not a recording of the SP. The pauses explain the checks and do not represent measured transfer times. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Start with a transfer that cannot install anything

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Moving firmware by SD card slowed every iteration. Before adding a persistent writer, we built R9 to answer a smaller question: could our original application enumerate on Windows and receive a complete, bounded program over USB? Its protocol could upload bytes and check them in RAM. It had no flash or execution operation.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The first physical transfer contained 8,488 bytes. R9 reported that the received length, transport checksum and RAM-reread checksum agreed. A new host invocation read the same final status. That was useful transport evidence, but the PC had received a device verification result, not an independent dump of those memory bytes. Nothing had been installed, and the uploaded program had never run.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A successful upload needs a precise destination. Record whether the bytes are in RAM, persistent storage, or a running program.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Let a compatibility failure stop the write

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R10 added a writer whose runtime lived in RAM while it worked on the application region. Its first read-only probe stopped with error 11. No erase or program command had been sent. The surrounding checks had passed, but R10 could not export enough diagnostic detail to identify the exact failing table condition from that result alone.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The suspected mismatch was the flash chip's SFDP table, which describes supported memory operations. R10 required at least eleven words; a documented older profile used nine. A synthetic regression reproduced the rejection, so we kept the failed package and built R11 with a narrow diagnostic export and support for that specific profile. We did not disable the preflight check to make the test proceed.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Capture the profile before trusting the correction

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R11's physical capture matched the documented nine-word table. That resolved the earlier hypothesis: R10's minimum-length guard had rejected the actual device profile. The shared identification code still did not establish an exact chip part number, and accepting this profile did not establish compatibility with other chips.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We then used a separate proof program with a different visible title and build marker. Its 11,716 bytes occupied three storage sectors. R11 reported 12,288 programmed and verified bytes because the last sector also contained padding. The readback compared every occupied-sector byte with the staged image or expected padding before publishing success. A checksum alone would have been a weaker description of what this writer checked.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Identify the running writer and its supported image format.

2. Check the measured device profile against the candidate's requirements.

3. Keep the new program's identity distinct from the writer currently running.

4. Require complete readback and an independently opened status check.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: These are evidence requirements, not instructions to install a package. The historical writer accepted only its bounded application format.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Treat the restart as a separate test

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Storage completion left the base R11 runtime alive in RAM. Its continued USB response could not tell us whether the newly stored program would start. The owner performed a real power cycle and reported the new title, USB BOOT R11. A fresh USB read then returned the proof marker 523B0002 with idle state and cleared transfer state.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: That pair of observations closed this particular update: the owner saw the intended program and the host independently read its new identity after restart. We preserved the upload, flash and boot records separately so a later reader could distinguish device-side storage verification from the subsequent boot. A process exit code or a progress screen could not replace those records.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The exercise below models a report collector. Each event proves one additional condition, and a boot is accepted only when its identity matches the intended target. Try moving the boot event earlier or changing its marker. Both should fail, even if all bytes were received.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: One successful R11 update established a working route for that bounded application format on this SP. It left repeat-update endurance, power-loss behavior and larger images untested. A host reconnect was also not a cable-reconnect test. Keeping these limits attached to the result prevented the first success from becoming a broader recovery claim.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Run this standalone Python 3 model. It uses invented events in memory, accepts no firmware or device input, and writes no files.

1/5 received
2/5 ram_checked
3/5 stored
4/5 status_checked
old identity: rejected
5/5 booted

text.name: Evidence label

Device readback and fresh boot identity
September 22, 2026

text.name: Article title
text.text: From a RAM upload to a booted update

text.name: Description
text.text: How a working USB connection became a verified persistent update, with a failed compatibility check in between.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R9 received a program into memory. R11 eventually stored a different program and booted it. We needed separate evidence for every step between those two results.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: After a real restart, the owner saw USB BOOT R11 and USB reported the proof's distinct marker with fresh idle state.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic status sequence, not a recording of the SP. The pauses explain the checks and do not represent measured transfer times. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Start with a transfer that cannot install anything

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Moving firmware by SD card slowed every iteration. Before adding a persistent writer, we built R9 to answer a smaller question: could our original application enumerate on Windows and receive a complete, bounded program over USB? Its protocol could upload bytes and check them in RAM. It had no flash or execution operation.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The first physical transfer contained 8,488 bytes. R9 reported that the received length, transport checksum and RAM-reread checksum agreed. A new host invocation read the same final status. That was useful transport evidence, but the PC had received a device verification result, not an independent dump of those memory bytes. Nothing had been installed, and the uploaded program had never run.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A successful upload needs a precise destination. Record whether the bytes are in RAM, persistent storage, or a running program.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Let a compatibility failure stop the write

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R10 added a writer whose runtime lived in RAM while it worked on the application region. Its first read-only probe stopped with error 11. No erase or program command had been sent. The surrounding checks had passed, but R10 could not export enough diagnostic detail to identify the exact failing table condition from that result alone.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The suspected mismatch was the flash chip's SFDP table, which describes supported memory operations. R10 required at least eleven words; a documented older profile used nine. A synthetic regression reproduced the rejection, so we kept the failed package and built R11 with a narrow diagnostic export and support for that specific profile. We did not disable the preflight check to make the test proceed.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Capture the profile before trusting the correction

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R11's physical capture matched the documented nine-word table. That resolved the earlier hypothesis: R10's minimum-length guard had rejected the actual device profile. The shared identification code still did not establish an exact chip part number, and accepting this profile did not establish compatibility with other chips.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We then used a separate proof program with a different visible title and build marker. Its 11,716 bytes occupied three storage sectors. R11 reported 12,288 programmed and verified bytes because the last sector also contained padding. The readback compared every occupied-sector byte with the staged image or expected padding before publishing success. A checksum alone would have been a weaker description of what this writer checked.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Identify the running writer and its supported image format.

2. Check the measured device profile against the candidate's requirements.

3. Keep the new program's identity distinct from the writer currently running.

4. Require complete readback and an independently opened status check.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: These are evidence requirements, not instructions to install a package. The historical writer accepted only its bounded application format.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Treat the restart as a separate test

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Storage completion left the base R11 runtime alive in RAM. Its continued USB response could not tell us whether the newly stored program would start. The owner performed a real power cycle and reported the new title, USB BOOT R11. A fresh USB read then returned the proof marker 523B0002 with idle state and cleared transfer state.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: That pair of observations closed this particular update: the owner saw the intended program and the host independently read its new identity after restart. We preserved the upload, flash and boot records separately so a later reader could distinguish device-side storage verification from the subsequent boot. A process exit code or a progress screen could not replace those records.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The exercise below models a report collector. Each event proves one additional condition, and a boot is accepted only when its identity matches the intended target. Try moving the boot event earlier or changing its marker. Both should fail, even if all bytes were received.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: One successful R11 update established a working route for that bounded application format on this SP. It left repeat-update endurance, power-loss behavior and larger images untested. A host reconnect was also not a cable-reconnect test. Keeping these limits attached to the result prevented the first success from becoming a broader recovery claim.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Run this standalone Python 3 model. It uses invented events in memory, accepts no firmware or device input, and writes no files.

text.name: Command
text.text:
1/5 received
2/5 ram_checked
3/5 stored
4/5 status_checked
old identity: rejected
5/5 booted

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: The invented identity check represents the distinction between a writer still running in RAM and a newly booted target. It does not implement a USB protocol or qualify any real image.

text.name: Evidence text
text.text:
Device readback and fresh boot identity. The reports below are retained project records; their underlying files are not published here. Read the curated evidence record.

One physical update and boot, on the owner's SP.

Device-side readback was not an independent external-flash dump.

The historical writer was limited to compatible application images up to 64 KiB.

Power-loss recovery, repeat-update endurance and sampler functionality were not established.

text.name: Evidence label
text.text:
Full-size readback and retained writer
September 24, 2026

text.name: Article title
text.text: A USB writer that survives the update

text.name: Description
text.text: Why installing a working application removed its updater, and how the B1 bridge kept a writer available afterward.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The first full-size USB update worked, then the USB writer disappeared. It belonged to the application we had just replaced.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: The owner confirmed A1, then a later writer boot returned B1's fresh idle identity.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic boot paths. These screens explain component ownership and are not device captures or installation instructions. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Move beyond the small proof image

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The early original applications fit inside a 64 KiB writer limit. Restoring the working R3 sampler required a much larger image: 2,652,672 bytes. R16B provided a full-size transfer path, and we checked the RAM upload separately before asking its writer to modify storage.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The earlier R16 package lacked a USB-reset preservation correction and remained excluded from this test. Even identifying R16B needed care: an apparent restart initially left the old runtime and its completed transfer state alive. After another full power cycle, a fresh R16B marker and idle state confirmed the intended starting point. That check kept the test attached to the corrected build.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Keep the same evidence standard at a larger size

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The first stage received all R3 bytes into RAM with a matching checksum and no programmed bytes. The persistent stage then reported 2,654,208 bytes programmed and read back, including sector padding. A separately opened status check repeated the completed result and checksum. Increasing the size did not remove the need to verify every occupied sector.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The writer still ran from RAM after storage completed. Only a real restart could test the stored application. The owner replied that R3 worked after that cycle. We recorded this as owner-reported startup; the brief reply did not quote the exact marker. The readback record establishes the device writer's comparison, not an independent inspection of the flash chip.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The extra 1,536 bytes belong to sector padding. Comparing the image length with the verified storage length should account for that difference.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Find out which program contains the updater

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Once R3 was running, R16B's USB writer was gone. The update had replaced the application that supplied it. A successful USB installation therefore did not guarantee another USB installation would be possible from the resulting program.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: B1 addressed that ownership problem by putting two entry paths inside a stock-based application package. Ordinary startup continued to the sampler; a separate writer startup entered B1. The bridge needed one initial SD installation because the running R3 application did not already provide that route. B1 was still part of the application image. It did not replace the resident loader or establish recovery after damage to that loader.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Locate the writer in the currently running package.

2. Check whether the replacement package also contains a compatible writer.

3. Verify the normal application after restart.

4. Verify the retained writer in a separate fresh startup.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: An updater included in the outgoing image cannot provide the next update once that image has been replaced.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Verify the sampler and the writer separately

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner reported installing the B1-wrapped R3 package, then saw USB BRIDGE B1 on its writer startup. The PC independently confirmed its marker, idle state and passing read-only preflight. We used that route to install the B1-wrapped A1 diagnostic application.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A1's 2,671,332-byte image occupied 653 sectors. B1 reported 2,674,688 bytes programmed and verified, followed by a separate matching status read. After normal startup, the owner explicitly confirmed AUDIO TAP A1 and its receive-position display. A subsequent writer startup returned USB BRIDGE B1, and the PC saw fresh idle state with cleared transfer counters. This last check established that A1 retained the writer; A1's normal screen alone could not establish it.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Model the package before discussing recovery

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The exercise represents each application as a set of components. Replacing that set explains why the first writer vanished and why a wrapped package could retain one. Change the target components and check whether the next update remains available. This is a packaging model, without a flash driver or device connection.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: B1 improved the normal update workflow, but it did not make a write atomic. Keeping the first application sector until last reduced one vulnerable interval without preserving the old body during a partial write. The later partial-update incident made that limitation concrete. A retained application writer and an independent recovery route need separate qualification.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Track the writer through a replacement

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: This Python 3 exercise uses invented packages represented by in-memory sets. It performs no installation, network access or file writes.

text.name: Command
text.text:
lab: writer available
sampler: writer absent
wrapped: writer available
replacement inherits only its own components

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: A real package also needs compatible formats, memory ownership and qualified hardware behavior. The model checks only whether a component survives replacement.

text.name: Evidence text
text.text:
Full-size readback and retained writer. The reports below are retained project records; their underlying files are not published here. Read the curated evidence record.

B1 resides in the application image and is not independent resident recovery.

A full readback result does not make the write atomic.

The initial bridge required an SD installation.

The historical success applies to the tested wrapped packages and this SP.

Failed write and owner/USB recovery evidence
September 25, 2026

text.name: Article title
text.text: What a partial update taught us

text.name: Description
text.text: A cumulative work limit stopped a write partway through. The failure changed how we budget operations and report success.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R31 never booted. Its transfer reached RAM, then the writer stopped after reporting only part of the application programmed. We preserved that failure and recovered the earlier R27 application.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: After the owner's application-only SD recovery, the screen and fresh USB marker identified R27.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic incident sequence. Progress values come from the retained device reports; sector contents were not independently dumped. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Heading
text.text: A completed request can still report failure

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Before the partial write, R30 exposed a smaller reporting mistake. A requested provider diagnostic failed and placed its coordinator in HOLD. The host process nevertheless exited successfully because the USB exchange had completed. Its decoded report already said the provider had failed; the process result disagreed with the operation result.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We preserved the original host tool and made a separate correction that returned a failing exit status for a failed requested diagnostic. Captured-transfer replay checked the change without touching the device. The owner then removed power completely, and a fresh USB read confirmed R30 back in idle state. The later write attempt began from that fresh session, not from the earlier HOLD.

text.name: Heading
text.text: The whole file arrived, but the write did not finish

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The R31 candidate was 27,300 bytes. The device received every byte, then stopped its persistent operation with state 7 and error 30. Only 20,480 bytes were reported programmed. A separately opened status read agreed with the failure and progress count. The candidate never reached final full-sector readback or a confirmed boot.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The exhausted limit counted work across the entire operation. Individual waits could be finite and reasonable while their accumulated cost exceeded the shared allowance. Earlier models had made the memory respond immediately, so they missed this interaction. The failure exposed a gap in the test model as well as in the writer's budgeting.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Received length, programmed progress, verified length and boot identity are different fields. None can stand in for the others.

text.name: Heading
text.text: An old entry point does not preserve the old application

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The writer saved the first application sector until last. Applying that order to the reported progress suggested that the entry sector was still old while part of the body had changed. This was an inference from the implementation and status, not a readback of the failed image. The uncertain sector was kept explicitly uncertain.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Even if the old entry bytes remained, they could call into a mixed old/new body. We therefore could not call the stored result either a valid R30 or a valid R31. The failure record remained attached to R31, with no normal-boot success claim. Clearing a status or restoring controller settings would not have repaired those application bytes.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Record exactly what the recovery proves

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner first reached an SD updater screen that listed both application packages. We stopped before proceeding because the intended restore concerned only the main application. After correcting the card contents, the owner reported the application-only updater and its completion message, then ROM MAP R27 on normal startup.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A fresh USB read independently confirmed R27's marker 524D0001 with idle state. This established physical recovery from the partial main-application write through the intact resident update path. The owner prepared the card on another computer, and we did not independently read it back here. The SD operation also did not supply the full flash readback used by our USB writer. Damage to the resident loader or APP0 remained outside this result.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Give each bounded operation its own allowance

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The separate Writer B component gives each size-bounded operation a fresh allowance at its outer boundary. Inner polling loops cannot refill it. Cleanup has an independent allowance, so an operation that runs out of work units can still make a bounded attempt to observe the memory becoming idle before restoring controller state.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Its compiled models include finite slow responses and a permanently busy device with a frozen timer. They keep the first error even when cleanup later succeeds. Those are offline tests; Writer B was not established as a physically validated repair or a new installable package by this work. The small exercise below reproduces the budgeting distinction without representing memory, sectors or an actual writer.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Bound jobs without starving later jobs

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Use Python 3 to compare cumulative and per-job limits on invented costs. The example runs entirely in memory and does not communicate with hardware or write files.

text.name: Command
text.text:
one allowance: 2/3 jobs
bounded allowances: 3/3 jobs
oversized job rejected: True
cleanup can finish: True
original failure remains recorded

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: Real bounds also cover nested work and a maximum number of jobs. Giving every loop unlimited new fuel would destroy the bound. Cleanup completion cannot turn a partially completed operation into success.

R31 never booted and its partial storage contents were not independently dumped.

The recovery establishes an intact-resident application restore, not independent resident recovery.

The owner prepared the recovery card elsewhere; its contents were not independently read back here.

Writer B's correction was tested in compiled models, not qualified on the SP by this incident.

text.text: An old entry point does not preserve the old application

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The writer saved the first application sector until last. Applying that order to the reported progress suggested that the entry sector was still old while part of the body had changed. This was an inference from the implementation and status, not a readback of the failed image. The uncertain sector was kept explicitly uncertain.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Even if the old entry bytes remained, they could call into a mixed old/new body. We therefore could not call the stored result either a valid R30 or a valid R31. The failure record remained attached to R31, with no normal-boot success claim. Clearing a status or restoring controller settings would not have repaired those application bytes.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Record exactly what the recovery proves

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner first reached an SD updater screen that listed both application packages. We stopped before proceeding because the intended restore concerned only the main application. After correcting the card contents, the owner reported the application-only updater and its completion message, then ROM MAP R27 on normal startup.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A fresh USB read independently confirmed R27's marker 524D0001 with idle state. This established physical recovery from the partial main-application write through the intact resident update path. The owner prepared the card on another computer, and we did not independently read it back here. The SD operation also did not supply the full flash readback used by our USB writer. Damage to the resident loader or APP0 remained outside this result.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Give each bounded operation its own allowance

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The separate Writer B component gives each size-bounded operation a fresh allowance at its outer boundary. Inner polling loops cannot refill it. text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Its compiled models include finite slow responses and a permanently busy device with a frozen timer. They keep the first error even when cleanup later succeeds. text.name: Description
text.text: A bounded program ran from RAM and returned to the updater without an owner power cycle. R37 made that round trip observable.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Uploading a program was already possible. R37 tested the harder round trip: admit one known program, run it, reset normally, and confirm the updater came back.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: Fresh R37 USB, the expected result and a separate writer preflight confirmed the round trip without an owner power cycle.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic R37 sequence, not recorded screen footage. The historical test used a fixed original payload; this page does not accept or execute programs. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Timeline title
text.text: Follow one program through the round trip

text.name: Heading
text.text: Make execution produce evidence after it ends

text.name: Paragraph

An accepted launch request might precede a crash, a stalled controller or a program that never reaches its intended entry. We needed a result that could be checked after the original application returned.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R37 used one fixed original program, 4,304 bytes long, with an expected retained result and a guarded normal watchdog reset. Restricting the payload made the first physical qualification small enough to reason about. The goal was this particular warm round trip. text.name: Heading
text.text: Avoid rebuilding a working connection during admission

text.name: Paragraph

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The staging buffer had one owner at a time. Once RAM mode was admitted, ordinary writer commands could not use that memory, and the writer would reject the RAM status format. A fault or cancellation kept the route closed until restart, avoiding an improvised return to a writer that might inherit uncertain buffer state. The successful revision did not, by itself, identify the exact underlying cause of the earlier transition failures.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A shared memory region needs explicit ownership. Two individually correct services can still corrupt each other when they use the same buffer concurrently.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Read each state before taking the next step

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: After the owner confirmed LOADER LAB R37, a fresh USB read identified the expected application in idle state. RAM admission returned its own status format on the same connection. text.name: Paragraph

These checks established that the intended program was admitted and ready; they did not establish execution. We kept the launch record distinct from the later return record so the host could not report success merely because the request was sent.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Identify the fresh original application.

2. Confirm exclusive admission to its bounded RAM test mode.

3. Check the sealed result independently of the transfer request.

4. Evaluate execution from the post-return evidence, not the launch acknowledgment.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Check both the program result and the updater

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The physical execution record found R37 back in fresh normal state with the exact retained result expected from the fixed program. The reset status changed from its initial value of 1 to 17, consistent with the intended normal watchdog reset. No owner power cycle occurred during this test, which separated the automatic return from a manual recovery.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A further read-only check confirmed the normal updater and its passing chip/profile preflight after return. No flash command was sent by that check. Together, the matching payload result, fresh application state and functioning updater established more than a surviving USB connection. The test also left the resident loader, APP0 and boot fuses unchanged.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Reproduce admission and cancellation without a device

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The model below names the current memory owner and permits one transition at a time. It rejects a writer request while RAM mode owns the buffer. A second run demonstrates cancellation: a cancelled session cannot silently fall back into writer ownership without a reset. Try removing that restriction to see which assertion stops protecting the shared state.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: This ownership exercise contains no program loader or execution operation. The hardware result remains one successful warm path using the pinned original payload. Repeated-run endurance, interrupted admission, compatibility with other payloads and every power-management case need their own physical evidence before they can become supported behavior.

text.text: Give a shared buffer one owner

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: This standalone Python 3 state model uses invented mode names and no hardware, network, program input or file output.

admitted: ram
concurrent writer: rejected
fixed test: returned
after reset: writer
cancelled session: reset required

text.name: Evidence label
text.text:
Captured windows and owner-reported correlation
September 22 to 24, 2026

text.name: Article title
text.text: When moving counters were not sound

text.name: Description
text.text: How frozen receive windows, corrected comparisons and a known input separated bus activity from changing audio.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The receiver counted roughly 768,000 words per second. Its first frozen windows still contained a fixed pattern. We had to compare matching positions and account for dropped words before assigning any audio meaning.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: With B1-wrapped A1, the owner reported raw positions responding to the audible rear-input source.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic receive investigation. Values illustrate the documented checks; the animated display is not a recording or a measured audio waveform. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Heading
text.text: A busy receiver can carry a fixed pattern

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R14's counters were consistent with about 768,000 receive words and 48,000 word-start observations per second. Sixteen words per frame fit those rates. The measurements established activity under the test conditions, but they did not identify physical input slots or prove that samples changed with sound.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: An adjacent-word change counter also rose as the receiver progressed. R15 added frozen windows so we could inspect that interpretation. Its first twelve windows each contained two groups of sixteen words. Comparing each position with the matching position in the next group gave zero changes across 192 comparisons. A repeating pattern can change between adjacent positions while staying identical from frame to frame.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Reject comparisons whose position reference has moved

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The windows contained zeros and a repeated pair of 0000FFFF values. Their positions lined up using the receiver's software count modulo sixteen. That count was an arbitrary reference, so we did not label it a physical channel number.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A later tone capture appeared to contain 512 values outside the idle baseline. It also had two FIFO overruns where the earlier baseline had none. Lost words were not included in the software count, so its phase could shift relative to the incoming stream. The comparison was invalid. We preserved the original result and made the corrected tool reject that pair. Subsequent same-session comparisons with stable error counters found the pattern unchanged.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Compare the same positions only when their alignment is trustworthy. Error counters belong to the evidence, not just the diagnostics footer.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Correct the input setup before blaming the hardware

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The owner initially supplied a 440 Hz tone through the front input, then clarified the connector. The intended comparison used rear LINE IN. After moving the source to rear L/MONO without restarting, another valid comparison still found no values outside the baseline.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R15 had no stock EXT SOURCE routing action, transmitter setup or codec initialization. Its unchanged receive pattern therefore could not diagnose a failed rear jack or a silent converter. We returned to the stock-based R3 sampler to establish an audible source path. The first rear-input attempt was silent; the owner later heard the tone through SP headphones after raising the source interface's rear MONITOR control, with SP input LEVEL reported as 127.

text.name: Heading

text.name: Article title
text.text: The timeout that wasn't a stalled stream

text.name: Description
text.text: A first-fault snapshot exposed a timestamp race. R41 then sustained silent streaming, while audible output remained a separate test.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The stream reported no progress shortly after a completed block. Capturing the state before shutdown showed that the timeout calculation could read its two timestamps in the wrong order.

text.name: Stage explanation
text.text: R41 reached 44,998 silent blocks without reported audio, DMA, FIFO or sync faults. Audibility was not confirmed.

text.name: Stage scope
text.text: Schematic progression from R38 to R41. Block counts and the 71-tick snapshot interval are documented results; playback speed is illustrative. Illustrative timing; no device connection.

text.name: Timeline title
text.text: Preserve the fault before changing the stream

text.name: Heading
text.text: Qualify the transport before asking for sound

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The original audio application started with output disabled. Its first active test moved zero-valued data, which let us examine the stream without treating an audible waveform as the only sign of progress. R38 reached its DMA interrupt handler, caught a transmit FIFO error and stopped before counting a healthy block. The USB writer remained responsive.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Empty transmit FIFOs at startup were a plausible cause, but the record did not capture the timing needed to prove it. R39 tested that hypothesis by filling the FIFOs with zeros before enabling the stream. It kept the existing fault checks. The physical attempt advanced through 31 healthy block completions before a different error, a no-progress timeout, stopped it.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Save first-fault state before cleanup destroys it

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R39's clean flags described its last completed interrupt, not necessarily the later moment when the timeout fired. They could not exclude a fault after that interrupt or explain why progress appeared to stop. Repeating the same test would not recover the missing state.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R40 added a fixed first-fault snapshot before shutting down the audio hardware. It recorded the relevant DMA, FIFO and interrupt state without clearing the fault on read. Its physical attempt counted thirteen healthy blocks, then reported the timeout again. The snapshot began only 71 timer ticks after the latest block, with DMA still active and no reported DMA error. That interval directed attention to the timeout calculation itself.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A status captured during the last good event cannot fully describe a later failure. Preserve the failure state before resetting the subsystem.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Two valid reads can form an impossible interval

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R40 read the current timer first, then the timestamp of the latest completed block. An interrupt could finish a block between those reads and update the latter timestamp. The calculation would then subtract a newer timestamp from an older current-time sample. In unsigned arithmetic, that small negative difference becomes a very large elapsed interval.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R41 reads the last-block timestamp before reading the current clock. A deterministic test ran both compiled images with the problematic interrupt interleaving: it reproduced the R40 timeout and kept R41 running. Separate checks retained genuine-timeout behavior and handled timer rollover. The correction therefore addressed the read order without removing the timeout that detects real loss of progress.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Keep the model result separate from the hardware result

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: R41's installation passed full occupied-sector readback and a separately opened status check. After the owner reported restarting, a fresh USB identity confirmed the new build with audio off and an idle writer. Those checks established the test baseline; the compiled race regression alone could not establish sustained physical streaming.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The silent run advanced through separated observations and ultimately reached 44,998 blocks without an audio, DMA, FIFO or sync fault. A single bounded waveform request also completed, and its timed lease returned the link to idle without error. The owner changed focus before reporting audibility or pressing pad 1. We therefore recorded sustained transport and a completed bounded request, while leaving headphone routing and pad-triggered sound unconfirmed.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text:
1. Confirm the corrected build after a real restart.

2. Observe silent progress across separate checks.

3. Keep the bounded waveform result distinct from a listening report.

4. Retain the failed binaries and snapshots alongside the correction.

text.name: Heading
text.text: Reproduce the unsigned timeout in memory

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The exercise uses an invented eight-bit timer so wraparound fits on one line. It supplies the two reads from the bad interleaving, then checks an ordered pair, a real timeout and a legitimate timer rollover. The bit width and numbers are teaching values, not the device's measured clock.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Reading the timestamps in the corrected order addresses this particular race. It does not prove that any two shared values are safe to read independently, or that a sequential fault snapshot is instantaneous while DMA continues. R41's physical result extends the evidence beyond the CPU model, but it still does not establish sampler features, audio quality or an audible output route.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Run this Python 3 model of an invented wrapping timer. It has no device input, network operations or file writes.

text.name: Command
text.text:
racing reads: age=255, timeout=True
ordered reads: age=3, timeout=False
real timeout: age=41, timeout=True
timer rollover: age=9, timeout=False

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: The example exposes the arithmetic consequence of a stale current-time read. The real correction also had compiled interleaving tests and a later physical silent-stream result.

text.text:

No pad-triggered sound result was recorded.
